linux.mechanism: efivarfs reads of /sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SecureBoot-* and SetupMode-* (4-byte attributes + 1 data byte; errno-classified absent/unreadable)

macos.fallback: no public API; SIP reported under code_integrity

caveats: **A container without `/sys/firmware/efi` reads Secure Boot as `absent`, even on a Secure Boot host.** The mount check separates "mounted, but this value is absent" from "the surface is not mounted" for the securityfs reads, but not for efivarfs: a default container's `/sys` tree omits `/sys/firmware/efi` whatever the host's firmware, and neither `deploy/docker/Dockerfile.agent` nor the repository's compose files bind-mount it. Closing this needs a deploy-side change (bind-mounting `/sys/firmware/efi` read-only into the agent container), and the Linux sample, a container capture, shows exactly this on its two `secure_boot` rows.

**Configured policy, not runtime proof.** The Windows rows read registry values, which say what is configured. Whether Device Guard, HVCI or Credential Guard is actually running is a separate runtime fact (`Win32_DeviceGuard`) that this plugin does not query, and it does not call WLDP.

**macOS `secure_boot` is unsupported, and `code_integrity` parses tool text.** There is no public API for the boot-security policy and `bputil` is a recovery-environment tool that is not run, so `secure_boot` always reports `UNAVAILABLE` on a Mac. Gatekeeper and SIP have no library API either, so both are read from a tool's text: the parsers match an exact line and report anything else as `unmodelled`. Security.framework `SecStaticCode*` is not used, because every call in that family validates one named code object's own signature, not a machine-wide enforcement setting.

**Fixed reads, no discovery.** The plugin reads only the keys named above; it does not walk securityfs or the registry (apart from listing the value names under `CI\Policy`), and it does not report TPM or measured-boot state.

**Windows `CI\Policy` is listed whole but modelled for one value.** Every value under the key appears as a row, but only `VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState` has a state mapping; the others (for example `SkuPolicyRequired`) read `unmodelled` with the raw number, which says the value exists, not what it means.

definitions.description: Reports code-signing enforcement posture. Linux reads the active LSM list and the kernel lockdown mode; macOS runs `spctl --status` (Gatekeeper) and `csrutil status` (SIP); Windows reads the Code Integrity policy, Device Guard, HVCI and Credential Guard (LsaCfgFlags) registry values, plus every value under CI\Policy. A value the OS definitively lacks reads `absent`, which is not a failure; a read that failed reads `unreadable` and downgrades the result to CONSTRAINED/PARTIAL (PERMISSION_DENIED/PARTIAL when refused) rather than failing the command.

Reports whether UEFI Secure Boot is enforced. Linux reads the efivarfs SecureBoot and SetupMode variables (two rows); Windows reads UEFISecureBootEnabled under Control\SecureBoot\State (one row); macOS has no public API and reports one `unsupported` row. A host with no efivars (BIOS or CSM boot) reads `absent`, which is a normal answer and not a failure; a variable that exists but could not be read reads `unreadable` and downgrades the result to CONSTRAINED/PARTIAL (PERMISSION_DENIED/PARTIAL when the read was refused) rather than failing the command.

description: Secure Boot and code-integrity enforcement posture (read-only)
how_it_works:
Two read-only actions report whether boot-time and code-signing protections are configured on: `secure_boot` (is Secure Boot enforced) and `code_integrity` (is the OS restricting what code may run). Each writes rows of the form `<action>|<os>|<key>|<raw>|<state>`. Neither takes parameters, so no request text reaches a path, a registry name or a command line. Linux reads a few efivarfs and securityfs files; Windows reads registry values; macOS reports `secure_boot` as unsupported and runs `spctl --status` and `csrutil status` for `code_integrity`. Every read is a **value** with a state, **`absent`** (the OS definitively says it is not there) or **`unreadable`** (the read failed), and a failed read never reads as absent. `enabled`, `disabled` and `partial` describe the protection, not the raw number. The Windows rows report configured policy, not proof of what is running.

This plugin's priority is asserted, not evidenced: it was built from a reading of a capability gap, and no capability-map requirement, parity gap, compliance control, roadmap item or named customer asks for it.
name: platform_security

columns.description: Row family: `code_integrity` (one per key read) or `constrained` (an internal-error row: the two-field row `constrained|internal_error`, which carries no os, key, raw or state).
columns.name: row_kind

columns.description: The leg that produced the row.
columns.name: os

columns.description: Value read: lsm and lockdown (Linux); gatekeeper and sip (macOS); ci_policy.<value name> for every value under CI\Policy, deviceguard.EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity, deviceguard.RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures, deviceguard.HypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity, deviceguard.hvci_scenario_enabled and lsa.LsaCfgFlags (Windows; LsaCfgFlags lives under Control\Lsa, not DeviceGuard).
columns.name: key

columns.description: The raw text or number read (the LSM list, the lockdown line with its bracketed active mode, the first line of tool output, or the registry value); "-" when nothing was read (absent or unreadable).
columns.name: raw

columns.description: enabled, disabled and partial describe the PROTECTION, not the raw value (Linux lockdown integrity is partial, confidentiality is enabled; macOS SIP with a custom configuration is partial). evaluation (Smart App Control in evaluation mode) and enabled_locked (Credential Guard with a UEFI lock) are Windows-only. unmodelled = a value was read that this table has no interpretation for (raw keeps it). absent = the OS definitively says it is not there (no lockdown LSM, no DeviceGuard values on a default Windows install), a normal answer and not a failure. unreadable = the read failed.
columns.name: state

columns.description: Row family: `secure_boot` (one per key read) or `constrained` (an internal-error row: the two-field row `constrained|internal_error`, which carries no os, key, raw or state).
columns.name: row_kind

columns.description: The leg that produced the row.
columns.name: os

columns.description: Value read: secure_boot and setup_mode (Linux efivars), secure_boot (macOS, unsupported row), UEFISecureBootEnabled (Windows).
columns.name: key

columns.description: The raw value read (the efivar data byte, or the registry DWORD as a number); "-" when nothing was read (absent, unreadable or unsupported).
columns.name: raw

columns.description: enabled = Secure Boot enforcing (for setup_mode: User Mode, a Platform Key is enrolled); disabled = Secure Boot off (for setup_mode: Setup Mode, no Platform Key, any image may load). The state describes the protection, not the raw number. unmodelled = a value was read that this table has no interpretation for (raw keeps it). absent = the OS definitively says it is not there (a BIOS/CSM boot has no efivars or SecureBoot\State), a normal answer and not a failure. unreadable = the read failed. unsupported = no mechanism on this OS (macOS).
columns.name: state

outputs_note:
Pipe-delimited rows written via `write_output()`, in read order. The first field is the fixed action literal (`secure_boot` or `code_integrity`), then `<os>`, `<key>`, `<raw>` and `<state>`. `<raw>` is `-` when nothing was read (`absent`, `unreadable`, `unsupported`); a raw value that was read passes through the shared untrusted-output escaper, which turns a backslash into `/` and escapes a pipe.

- **Row order.** Linux `secure_boot` writes `secure_boot` then `setup_mode`; Linux `code_integrity` writes `lsm` then `lockdown`; macOS writes `gatekeeper` then `sip`.
- **Windows row count.** Rows can outnumber the named values, because every `CI\Policy` value is listed, sorted by name, with the one modelled value mapped and the rest `unmodelled`.
- **Return codes.** The action returns 0 for every data-level outcome; an unknown action name returns 1 with the single row `unknown action: <name>`, and an internal exception returns 1 with the single two-field row `constrained|internal_error`.

privileges.grant: None documented for this plugin (`docs/agent-privilege-model.md`); HKLM `Control` reads are not expected to need elevation
privileges.if_refused: For a per-VALUE read, `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`/`ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND` reports the row `absent` with no token. For a KEY OPEN, the same two codes report `absent` only for `SecureBoot\State`, `CI\Policy`, `DeviceGuard` and its HVCI scenario subkey; `Lsa` has no evidenced not-found case, so the identical codes there report `unreadable` with `lsa:key_missing`. `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` reports `unreadable` with `<name>:access_denied` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`/`PARTIAL`; any other Win32 error reports `unreadable` with `<name>:win32_<n>`
privileges.measured: `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` on a bare-metal Windows 11 Pro host (10.0.26200), 2026-09-21: `SecureBoot\State` `UEFISecureBootEnabled` was 1 (Secure Boot on; the off state was never captured), `CI\Policy` held 4 `REG_DWORD` values, the `DeviceGuard`, HVCI and `LsaCfgFlags` values were absent (no VBS, HVCI or Credential Guard on state was ever measured); the sample is `docs/samples/windows.txt`

privileges.if_refused: A tool that cannot be started reports `unreadable` with `<key>:spawn_failed` (no errno) or `<key>:eacces` / `<key>:errno_<n>` (from the spawn errno, including a missing binary as `errno_2`); the other failures are `<key>:timeout`, `<key>:output_truncated`, `<key>:exit_<n>` and `<key>:exit_signal`
privileges.measured: Bare-metal Mac, unprivileged (euid 501), 2026-09-21: real capture (`docs/samples/macos.txt`); no root-privileged run has been captured
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, root today (LaunchDaemon carries no `UserName` key, see the `docs/agent-privilege-model.md` TL;DR); both tools need no elevation to report

privileges.if_refused: `EACCES`/`EPERM` reports the row `unreadable` with `<key>:eacces` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`/`PARTIAL`. `ENOENT` reports `absent` with no token only when the parent surface is confirmed present (securityfs mounted; for efivars, `/sys/firmware/efi` absent or efivarfs mounted); otherwise it is remapped to `ENODEV` and reports `unreadable` with `<key>:errno_19`. Any other errno reports `unreadable` with `<key>:errno_<n>`
privileges.measured: aarch64 Debian 13 container, root, 2026-09-23: real capture of the built `.so` (`docs/samples/linux.txt`). `secure_boot` reads `absent` (the gap in caveat 1) and `code_integrity` reads `unreadable` with `errno_19`, which the plugin reports when securityfs is not mounted, so the container is inferred to have no securityfs and no EFI variables (the mounts themselves were not recorded); no real Secure Boot value or lockdown mode has been captured
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, dedicated unprivileged account (the agent never runs as root on Linux)

result_status.when: No row was `unreadable`: every key was either read or `absent`. An `absent` row adds no reason token, so a BIOS host, a kernel without lockdown or a default Windows install still reports `OK`.

result_status.provenance: `no public API; SIP reported under code_integrity`
result_status.when: macOS `secure_boot`: the leg is unsupported by design and reports its `unsupported` row.

At least one row was `unreadable` and none was refused; one `<key>:<cause>` token per unreadable row, and `<key>:efivars:shape` is an efivar that is not 4 + 1 bytes. An `absent` row never appears here.
Any leg: an unexpected exception was contained in `execute()`; the action returns 1 with the row `constrained|internal_error`.

Any leg: a read was refused, `EACCES`/`EPERM` on Linux and for a macOS spawn, `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` on Windows. A refusal outranks every other unreadable cause in the same run; the reason still lists every unreadable row's token.

result_status.provenance: no public API; SIP reported under code_integrity

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`. Both actions are gathered definitions (`crossplatform.platform_security.secure_boot`, `crossplatform.platform_security.code_integrity`, 300s TTL).
**Not consumed by** daily-sync, TAR, DEX, or metrics.

**Sensitivity.** Rows carry boot-integrity and code-signing settings only: no username, path, process name or installed-software name. The values are a security-posture baseline of the host (for example Secure Boot off, Gatekeeper off, lockdown none), which tells an attacker where enforcement is weak, so the rows warrant the same handling as other `Security` data.

**Siblings:** `vuln_scan` (its configuration checks run `spctl --status` and `csrutil status` through `popen` as pass/fail findings; this plugin reports the raw text and a state over the bounded runner) and `bitlocker` (disk encryption posture).
